content: Merbromin, also known by various trade names such as Mercurochrome, Merbromine, Sodium mercurescein, Asceptichrome, Supercrome, Brocasept, and Cinfacromin, is a topical antiseptic primarily used for treating minor cuts and abrasions. It is a compound classified as an organomercuric disodium salt and a fluorescein derivative. While it remains widely available in many countries, its sale has been discontinued in Germany, the United States, and France due to concerns over its mercury content. The primary application of Merbromin is as a topical antiseptic. When applied to a wound, it imparts a bright red stain to the skin. In addition to its antiseptic properties, Merbromin is utilized as a biological dye for marking tissue margins and as a metal dye in industrial dye penetrant inspections to detect fractures in metals. Mercurochrome is a well-known trade name for Merbromin. Over-the-counter antiseptic solutions containing Merbromin, typically at a 2% concentration, are dissolved in either ethyl alcohol (tincture) or water (aqueous solution). The antiseptic properties of Merbromin were first identified in 1918 by Dr. Hugh H. Young, a physician at Johns Hopkins Hospital. It quickly gained popularity among parents and physicians for everyday antiseptic use, particularly for treating minor injuries in children. However, on October 19, 1998, the United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) reclassified Merbromin from the generally recognized as safe category to the untested category. This decision effectively halted its distribution in the United States due to concerns about potential mercury poisoning. Germany followed suit in 2003, and France banned its sale in 2006. Despite these restrictions, Merbromin remains readily available in most other countries. In the United States, products such as Humco Mercuroclear capitalize on the historical brand recognition of Mercurochrome but use alternative ingredients with similar properties. For example, Mercuroclear is an aqueous solution containing benzalkonium chloride and lidocaine hydrochloride, which serve as substitutes for Merbromin.
